references.text: Describes the actual execution of the cherubim on the mercy seat, with wings spread upward and faces turned toward each other, just as God commanded in Exodus 25:20.
The cherubim in Solomon's temple also had outstretched wings that covered a holy area, continuing the design of the tabernacle.
The cherubim in the temple spread their wings over the place where the ark stood and covered both the ark and its poles.
Describes the cherubim in Solomon's temple with outstretched wings reaching from wall to wall, based on the pattern of the tabernacle.
First mention of cherubim in the Bible, guarding the way to the tree of life. The cherubim are heavenly beings who guard holy places.
Ezekiel's vision of the cherubim above the dome, showing their role in God's presence.
Describes the wings of the cherubim as spread upward, similar to the cherubim on the mercy seat.
The New Testament refers to the cherubim of glory who overshadowed the place of atonement, a direct reference to the cherubim on the ark of the covenant.
The transition from tabernacle to temple shows the same theological function for the cherubim as bearers of God's holy presence.
The difference in the direction of the faces (toward the mercy seat versus toward the house) marks a theological nuance shifting focus from atonement to God's dwelling place.
The description of the unity between the cherubim and the mercy seat is essential for understanding their role as an inseparable part of God's throne of grace.
The structural similarity in the spreading of wings in Ezekiel's vision confirms the heavenly model underlying the holy spaces on earth.
